title: Directing an AI dev team for 3 weeks: architecture, workflow and failures from my pirate sailing game
author: DazedGenie
selftext:
**AI disclosure first:** I know how to code, but on this project I didnt write any of it myself. Claude wrote every line, all the tests, the dev tools and the blender scripts. The first 3d models came from Tripo and Meshy but those are all getting replaced with models built by blender scripts so they're ultimately removed. The painted art is ChatGPT and the sound effects, voices and music are ElevenLabs. My part is the design, the art direction, playtesting every build and deciding what gets merged. No AI runs while you play the game.

 The game is called **Canvas & Coin**. Its a pirate sailing sandbox inspired by the old Sid Meier's Pirates! and I have just released the first version of the demo here https://dazedgenie.itch.io/canvasandcoin

 Some numbers so you get the scale. The game currently runs on Godot 4 and GDScript only. Around 142k lines of game code, 58k lines of tests (over 2,600 test functions), 116k lines of blender python that build the models, about 280 models, 28 data files and close to 290 pull requests. All in roughly 3 weeks.

**The workflow**

 Before any code got written I spent a long time on a design doc. I started with a base idea and then would have Claude ask me multiple choice questions in rounds. Everything I picked got written down so it never has to guess what I meant.

 The real brain of the project is a file called CLAUDE.md that every session reads first. It has the engine version, the architecture rules, how coordinates work, how to run tests and take screenshots and a short note on every system. Any time a session learns something the hard way it goes in there. 

 I run a bunch of AI sessions at once and each one gets one job on its own branch. One feature or fix, one PR. There's a coordinator session that keeps track of all of them. Every PR has to open and run with F5 right after I pull it because I review by playing it, not by reading code.

 Every gameplay rule gets a test. The full suite takes 20 to 35 min so it runs on my PC instead of the cloud. I often work on my laptop and allow my desktop to solely run test.

 Claude also renders the game in its cloud container and looks at the screenshots itself before I ever see anything. There's a ton of command line flags just so it can set up any shot it wants, like put a storm here, dock there, start a boarding.


**The architecture**
 
- One sim owns the whole game. It ticks at a fixed 60 Hz and its the only code allowed to change game state. It knows nothing about meshes or UI.
- Pressing a key never touches a ship. It turns into a small command with a player id and the sim applies it next tick.
- Its deterministic. Same commands in the same order always give the same world. No clock, no global random, every roll is a hash of the seed, the day and a salt.
- That basically gave us co-op for free. The host sends each tick's commands, every guest replays them on their own copy and they compare a checksum every second. If a guest drifts it just asks for a fresh copy.
- Everything you see only reads the sim, it never writes back.
- Ships, ports, prices and balance all live in JSON with a schema for every field so mods can patch over it. A test fails if a field isn't in the schema.

 Having these as hard rules in CLAUDE.md matters more than anything else. The AI follows rules really well but its bad at coming up with an architecture halfway through.

**3D models from code**

 The first models (ships, people, creatures) were Tripo and Meshy generations that got fixed up in blender. They looked ok but were a pain to work with. Sails needed to be stripped and readded, mast beams needed to be removed, rudders would be seperated, Issues with LODS. They always needed a lot of work so I established a blender workflow that now handles all models. Ships, towns, forts, birds, sharks, whales and most of the legendary creatures are already built by blender python scripts on a shared kit. Hull lofts, named parts the game can rig, wear and shading baked into vertex colour, 3 levels of detail and a tool that checks for overlapping parts.

 For each model the AI works off a reference picture in a loop. Measure the picture, build, render, compare side by side, score it, fix, repeat. A second AI session does the judging so the builder isn't grading its own homework. Currently a basic new ship design takes about 20 minutes while the more unique ships can take up to an hour or more. The nice part is a change like "make all the hulls a bit chunkier" is just a rebuild now instead of re-sculpting everything.

**What went wrong**

- Model loops stall. Some models just stop getting better. A captain character got stuck around 5.8 out of 10 and a great white shark at 6.9. The fix is a stronger model, a better reference sheet or just calling it. Or improving upon the current workflow
- The cloud cant see everything. The container renders on the CPU and some effects like the see through shallow water just dont show up there, so those get judged on my GPU.
- Performance guesses were wrong. I figured the graphics card was the problem but measuring showed it was scripts on the CPU. A few passes took a busy sea scene from about 30 ms a frame down to 13. 
- Determinism is fragile. Godot's JSON parser loses digits on tiny floats and dictionary key order changes the checksum. Both broke co-op sync once and both are rules now.
- Merging before tests finish. I'm impatient and sometimes merge while CI is still running. A couple stale tests slipped through that way.
- The rules file keeps growing. Every lesson goes into CLAUDE.md so its huge now and every session has to read all of it. It needs splitting up.
- The art style and water in particular have changed a handful of times each already.

**What I'd tell someone starting out**

 1. Write the design down before any code and actually answer the AI's questions.
 2. Set hard architecture rules on day one and put them in the rules file.
 3. Make it test everything and review by playing.
 4. Have a second session check the first one's work.
 5. Keep every job small. One feature, one branch, one PR.

 Happy to answer anything about the setup. And if you try the demo theres a Feedback button in the pause menu that opens a short survey.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body: Totally agree on Meshy/Tripo based 3D models being totally unusable for a legitimate game. replies.author: DazedGenie
replies.body:
I will start off by saying everyones needs are different so results may vary. For my game primarily its buildings and boats which this method works rather well for. I've begun having more success with organics as of late through a lot of trial and error but I still cant create a high depth model like tripo. Slowly making progress in that direction though. If your curious about anything in particular feel free to ask and ill answer to the best of my ability.
________________________________________________________________________________________________

Every object goes through the same six steps.

1.  Plan. Start from a concept sheet (or a short written design). Decide the parts, sizes and triangle limit.
2.  Measure. Read the sizes off the drawing into numbers. Nothing is shaped by eye.
3.  Build. A script builds the model from a shared kit of parts.
4.  Check. Small scripts test the shape and triangle count. Then we render it in the game's look.
5.  Judge. A separate reviewer scores it against the target and lists what's wrong. We repeat until it scores 8 out of 10 or better.
6.  Export. A .glb goes in the game. A .blend is kept for editing. Approved ones go in my asset library.

The one rule: if a model is wrong, fix the script or its numbers, never the mesh by hand.
_______________________________________________________________________________________________

**What every script shares**

- Runs on its own. No Blender window needed. A --fast flag skips the slow lighting for quick tries.
- Kits. Each family (ships, creatures, houses) has a kit of shared parts. A model only adds what makes it different, so a whole fleet looks like one hand made it.
- Seeded randomness. Random numbers come from a seed, not the clock. Rebuilds match exactly, and adding a new piece never changes the old ones.
- Numbers from the concept art. Bodies, hulls and wings are shaped from tables of measurements. Change a number, rebuild.
- Flat painted look. Colour is vertex colour. Shade, sun fade and damp are baked in. The game adds the ink outlines and banded lighting.
- Limits. Every model has a triangle limit and a near, middle and far version. The build fails if it goes over.
- Named parts. Names are a contract with the game. SquareSail0 is a sail, Gun0 is a gun, Ensign is where a flag goes.
- Recipes. Parts we've solved are saved as short pages in tools/blender/recipes/ so the next model can reuse them.

______________________________________________________________________________________________
**Ships**

About 22 ship classes, plus four named ships, are built on one shipwright's kit. No ship is still on a generated model.

- Plan. Each ship gets a short design page before any code: what the old model got wrong, how she looks from the sailing camera, and her parts. Concept sheets are the target.
- Build. A recipe builds the hull from a table of measurements, then adds fittings like guns, masts, sails and rails. Each ship only keeps what makes her different. Shade, sun fade and tar are baked into the colours.
- Detail levels. Three per part. Planks are drawn wide, because thin seams turn into dots at normal camera distance.
- Check. A table lists triangles and doubled faces. A look script draws her in the game's materials from 35, 95 and 250 units. Yards and sails are swung through their full range to make sure nothing clips. Tests hold each hull to her size in the game data.
- Judge. A planner, a builder and a reviewer, with models Dazed picks. The named ships scored 8.0 to 9.0.
- Export. The .glb goes in assets/models/ships with the .blend beside it. ships.json names the model.

[Giving this to claude to see how to segment and measure things helped its generation a large amount as seen in the shark](https://imgur.com/a/4vMJ5Nm)
 
For my use case stopping with the wildlife at this point was fine but with this method you can essentially do as many loops as needed. After figuring out a particularly hard situation in blender I tell claude to remember for the future how it was resolved

comments.author: Exaweft
comments.body:
That's an interesting setup, especially the Blender side of things.

I like the idea of having one AI build the model and another review it. I'm curious though, how reliable have you found the scoring?

Does the reviewer generally pick up the same things you would, or do you still find yourself looking at an 8/10 model and thinking "yeah nah, that's definitely not an 8"? 😂

replies.author: DazedGenie
replies.body:
It really just depends on the context of what your looking at I guess. For my art style choice its a little more low poly cartoonish style so a 8/10 is a lot easier to come by vs some realistic rpg game.
_________________________________________________________________________________________
[Here is one of the unique ships in the game](https://imgur.com/a/E3MH4bD)

The judge scored her pass 7 out of 10 in four parts against the second measurement sheet, and the parts add to 8.4.

**Shape, 2.6 of 3**. Freeboards, draft, port rows, lantern height and lion size match the sheet, and the stern's underwater body now curves up to the sternpost. Points off because:
she's a bit short from the lion's tip to the gallery (about 1.14 of waterline length, against 1.20);
the taffrail sits a little low (0.25, against 0.28).

**Build, 2.5 of 3**. The mesh is clean: no doubled faces or overlaps, within the triangle budget, with three working detail levels. The quarter galleries cost points: from the side they read as one flat balustraded panel instead of three tiers stepping out as they go down. The forecastle's five small windows don't show either.

**Finish, 2.4 of 3**. The crimson and gold read well, crimson runs straight into copper as the sheet shows, and the stern looks rich at game distance. Points off because:
the lowest crimson strake is murky, so the third row of ports barely shows;
with the sea hidden, red streaks smear down into the copper, so the waterline isn't a clean line.

**Details, 0.9 of 1**. The crowned, roaring, rearing lion now reads from the side. The saltire, the three lanterns, the crest and the spritsail are all there. Points off because:
seen from ahead the lion is a thin gold column;
at the farthest detail level it's a blob.

**Still off:**
The lowest crimson strake is still murky.
Seen from ahead, the lion is a thin column.
From the side, the quarter galleries read flat.
___________________________________________________________________________

For my use where this ship will mainly be seen at a distance or from above I would say its a 8.4 Obviously if you were a harsher judge the reviewer could adjust accordingly. Usually if the loop gets stuck and returns 2 very similar scores or a regressed score it will request a effort increase or model swap. I'm currently looking into LLM and local generation so I've halted current iteration on this method until I determine if its worth continuing down or working through other software

comments.author: Extra-Appearance6541
comments.body:
The biggest thing Ive found for productivity is that documentation and branching appropriately is very important. If you have parts of the game that arn't fleshed out yet and you're trying to play around with ideas first you need to:

\* get rid of it when you're done, or

\* inform the AI very explicitly, and every time, that when making changes to ignore the spike code

Otherwise it treats it as ground truth, and shapes what you're asking it to do around it.

Another good habbit to get into is a fresh session redteaming a spec or plan that hasn't yet been executed (with an optional defender agent to argue back depending on architectural  importance), with whatever documentation you already have about the game, your intent, and current milestones. The stuff it catches can be crazy deep in the weeds and obscure but I've seen really critical issues come back out of it.

Working with AI in a less hands-on-code way reminds me of having a team of junior developers to manage again. But these ones are hooked up to a caffeine drip with encyclopaedic knowledge about obscure topics.

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body:
I find this a little surprising. I wonder what stopped you from looking at all the pirate games that are already out there. You could have just copied those mechanics since they are established and they work. That is exactly what I would have done. I have two games on Steam, and that is how I built them. I went in and copied proven, working game mechanics from the top games on Metacritic, then wrapped and baked them into my own ideas. And bingo - success! You guys do realize that you do not have to re-invent the wheel, right?

Top 15 Pirate Game Play Mechanics -

1. Seamless Ship to Shore Transitions: Sail across open water, drop anchor near an island or rival vessel, and step directly into swimming, diving, or deck to deck combat with no loading screens.
2. Broadside, Mortar, and Swivel Gun Combat: Aim heavy broadside cannons, lob long range explosive mortars, fire chain shots to snap masts, and use swivel guns or brass knuckles during close quarters.
3. Crippling and Boarding Takedowns: Disable an enemy ship's speed and armor until it goes dead in the water, then grapple across to complete boarding objectives like cutting flags, sniping officers, or blowing up powder kegs.
4. Ship Upgrades and Fleet Progression: Spend plundered metal, wood, and coin on hull armor, cannons, storage capacity, and crew quarters while dispatching captured ships on regional trade routes.
5. Crew Shanties and Wanted Level Escalation: Hear your crew sing contextual sea shanties as you sail, and manage your notoriety level as naval hunters pursue you across open waters.
6. Overland Wind, Speed, and Map Navigation: Steer your ship across the map using wind direction and sail trim while tracking shifting trade routes, ports, and national territories.
7. Fleet Composition and Crew Morale: Balance ship types from fast sloops to heavy galleons, divide loot among your crew, and keep morale high so men do not mutiny or desert.
8. Tactical Ship to Ship Duels: Maneuver for wind advantage, switch between cannonballs and grapeshot, and close distance to board enemy vessels.
9. Interactive Sword Fighting: Read opponent stances and strike patterns to time high slashes, low thrusts, parries, and ripostes on ship decks or in tavern duels.
10. Faction Reputation, Treasure Hunts, and Courtship: Play rival naval powers against each other, piece together treasure maps, and win over governors' daughters through dancing and gift giving.
11. Physical Crew Ship Operation: Manually raise or lower sails, angle them to catch the wind, turn the wheel, drop anchor, and patch hull breaches with planks while bailing water with buckets.
12. Manual Cannon Loading and Ballistics: Load cannonballs, chainshots, firebombs, or curseballs by hand, judge arc and wave motion, and fire while managing ammunition supplies.
13. Emergent PvPvE Risk Reward Loops: Carry physical loot chests, skulls, and cargo crates onto your ship where other crews can spot, chase, board, and steal your haul before you cash it in at an outpost.
14. Riddle Maps, X Marks the Spot, and Tall Tales: Decipher compass and pace clues, dig up buried chests, fight skeleton waves and sea monsters, or play structured story campaigns.
15. Harpoons, Rowboats, and Tool Radial: Use deck harpoons to snag loot, whip around tight corners, or dock rowboats, while swapping quickly between cutlass, flintlock or blunderbuss, spyglass, bucket, planks, and musical instruments.

replies.author: DazedGenie
replies.body: Obviously I looked at other games and what I like about them and try and make it work for me. I'm not really sure what you mean by trying to reinvent the wheel. All of the mechanics I have in the game are proven from other games so not sure what you are referring too. I've played other pirate games and always thought they were missing things so I'm making the game I've always wanted. I think the most valuable info I've shared is my blender process.

replies.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
replies.body: I am sure you will get it figured out in the future, maybe not this time, but next. All I meant by not reinventing the wheel is that for me personally, I just stick to tried and true established play mechanics. Things like using WASD to move, standard gamepad button layouts, and how people typically expect movement, running, jumping, combat, and interactions to feel.

replies.author: DazedGenie
replies.body: I just looked at the list you posted and I would say my game currently includes about 75% of the mechanics listed with the ones that aren't included being intentionally left out.

replies.author: DazedGenie
replies.body: I run everything through Claude code and use the project feature. I know it's not the most efficient and I'm most likely burning extra usage but I find it easy to track what's being worked on, what's done, what's planned and whatnot. I have Claude actively update a feature artifact that tracks the entire project and where each feature is at. I gave Claude access to my chatgpt so all artwork is automatically generated by Claude through chatgpt whenever needed. Ex: extra angles that are more detailed for modeling comparisons. Im currently in the planning phase of on my own framework to better combine Claude, codex, and Gemini all in one window for the future though. A good majority of the initial framework I layed out myself but honestly I don't think much of that still remains after all the optimization and changes since the initial creation
